extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on how to evaluate patent applications for compliance with statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and related procedural rules. Covers initial analysis, searching, claim interpretation, and forming and communicating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what invention is sought to be patented
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine precisely what the inventor has invented and is seeking to patent by reviewing the complete specification, detailed description, embodiments, the claims, and any asserted utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review. Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action, explain deficiencies clearly, indicate how rejections may be overcome when practicable, and fully develop reasons for non-prior-art rejections (e.g., written description, enablement, utility) rather than mere conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and understand any utility for the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention as a whole is useful and identify any asserted utility or practical application disclosed by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete disclosure should indicate why the applicant believes the invention is useful (the purpose or how it may be used). The statement of utility must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand why the invention is useful. Applicant may assert more than one utility but only one is necessary; alternatively, a well-established utility in the contemporaneous art may suffice. Note difference between 'practical application' for utility and 'practical application' in subject matter eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the written description and specific embodiments to understand what the applicant regards as the invention, its function, and the features necessary to accomplish an asserted practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine (A) the function of the invention (what it does when used as disclosed) and (B) the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application. Correlate disclosed embodiments to claim limitations to ensure proper interpretation and to support claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the claims (identify and evaluate each claim limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the property rights and must be carefully scrutinized by identifying each claim limitation and correlating each limitation to the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For process claims, identify steps/acts; for products, identify physical structures/materials. Correlate each claim limitation to portions of the specification that describe the limitation, including means-/step-plus-function language. Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure. Consider plain meaning, grammar, and how a person skilled in the art would understand terms. Be aware of language that may or may not be limiting (e.g., preamble statements of intended use, 'adapted to' clauses, 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, contingent limitations, printed matter, functional terms). Consider all claim limitations as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting claims during prosecution, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read positive limitations from the specification into claims that do not themselves impose that limitation. Means-/step-plus-function limitations should be interpreted consistently with corresponding structures/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Consider MPEP §§ 2111 and 2181–2186 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate claim limitations to supporting disclosure (including means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure each claim limitation has a corresponding disclosure in the specification; for means-/step-plus-function limitations, identify corresponding structure/materials/acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search must consider any structure or material described in the specification and equivalents corresponding to claimed means-/step-plus-function limitations per 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§ 2181–2186. If a limitation invokes 112(f), interpret to cover corresponding structure/materials/acts described and their equivalents; if disclosure lacks corresponding structure, consider indefiniteness or written description rejections and advise applicant how to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a thorough search of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Before evaluating patentability, examiners must perform a thorough search of prior art including both claimed and reasonably relevant unclaimed aspects described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search should take into account structures/materials and their equivalents corresponding to means-/step-plus-function limitations. Use guidance in MPEP §§ 904–904.03. Searching unclaimed aspects is important if there is reasonable expectation they may later be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (subject matter eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether it is directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature) unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the four interpreted requirements of §101 and related caselaw (e.g., Alice, Myriad, Chakrabarty, Bilski). Use the analytical framework and stepwise eligibility guidance in MPEP § 2106 (Eligibility Step 1: statutory categories; Eligibility Step 2A: whether directed to judicial exception; Eligibility Step 2B: whether amounts to significantly more). Avoid focusing solely on §101 to the detriment of §§102/103/112 analyses except in extreme cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1 — Identify statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm that the claimed subject matter falls within one of the four statutory categories set forth in 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not within a statutory category, the claim is not patent-eligible. See MPEP § 2106.03 for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A — Determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon/product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether the exception is integrated into a practical application (integration/prong one) and consider analyses such as markedly different characteristics, integration into practical application, particular machine/transformation, improvements to computer/technology, and particular treatment or prophylaxis as relevant indicators of integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2B — Determine whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, decide whether additional claim limitations in combination amount to significantly more than the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider improvements to computer functionality or other technology, particular machine or transformation, well-understood routine conventional activity, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use and technological environment, and other meaningful limitations. Use MPEP § 2106.05 and related subsections for examples and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness / claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention and whether the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention with reasonable precision and particularity in light of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claim language definiteness in light of the disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. Consider issues such as new terminology, relative terminology, numerical ranges, lack of antecedent basis, functional limitations, negative limitations, omnibus claims, multiple alternatives, and other specific topics identified in MPEP § 2173 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description, enablement, best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the three separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a): (A) adequate written description, (B) enablement, and (C) best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description: specification must reasonably convey that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date. Enablement: specification must enable one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation; consider undue experimentation factors, predictability of the art, quantity of experimentation, working examples, and special issues for biological/chemical/computer programming. Best mode: two-prong inquiry — did inventor possess a best mode at filing, and if so, is it disclosed so a skilled person could practice it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — specification must be enabling as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the specification enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention as of the filing date without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider art predictability, quantity of experimentation required, whether working examples are provided, whether critical information is missing, and whether enablement is commensurate in scope with the claims. For issues of operability and enablement in prior art rejections, follow MPEP §§ 2164 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) — prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting an obviousness rejection, establish a prima facie case by comparing claimed invention to prior art, identifying differences, determining level of ordinary skill, and showing motivation/suggestion to combine with reasonable expectation of success as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider analogous vs nonanalogous art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, level of ordinary skill, legal concept of prima facie obviousness, suggestion or motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success, consideration of applicant's rebuttal, and secondary considerations. All claim limitations must be considered; do not dissect claims into isolated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability and types (printed publication, patent, public use, on sale, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on prior art, determine whether a reference is available as prior art under the applicable statutory provision (AIA or pre-AIA), considering categories such as patents, printed publications, public use, on-sale activities, admissions, and foreign/domestic applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess level of public accessibility required for printed publications, date of availability, whether a patent document qualifies as a 'patent' for rejection purposes, status of unpublished or redacted applications, WIPO published applications, and distinctions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) and pre-AIA provisions. Use relevant MPEP chapters (2130s–2150s) for detailed criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 to overcome prior art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether affidavits/declarations can be used to overcome prior art rejections by showing inventor-originated disclosure, prior public disclosure by inventor, or derivation by another from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidance on who may file affidavits/declarations, situations when they are unavailable, showing disclosures by inventor or joint inventor, and use in establishing exceptions or antedating references (see MPEP §§ 2155–2156).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections; clearly communicate findings and bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Before making a rejection, confirm a prima facie case of unpatentability exists and clearly communicate findings, conclusions and the bases for them in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use applicable form paragraphs in Office actions to state bases for objections/rejections to reduce misunderstandings. Fully develop reasons especially for non-prior-art rejections (written description, enablement, utility) rather than mere conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution laches and res judicata considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether prosecution history laches or res judicata apply to bar claims or amendments based on unreasonable delay or prior final adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laches applies only in egregious cases of unreasonable and undue delay (e.g., repeated continuation filings with no substantive progress); obtain TC Director approval before rejecting on laches. Res judicata may preclude claims not patentably distinct from claims finally refused or canceled in prior administrative or court proceedings; apply carefully when prior decisions are final and no further court review is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) invocation and three-prong test for means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim limitation should be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph) using a three-prong analysis: whether the claim uses 'means' or a generic placeholder, whether it recites functional language, and whether it recites sufficient structure/material/acts to perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 112(f) applies, interpret the limitation to cover corresponding structure/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.30.05–7.30.07, 7.34.23–7.34.24) to explain invocation or non-invocation and to instruct applicant on possible responses (amend claims, show sufficient structure, or clarify record). If result of three-prong test is inconclusive, require applicant to clarify whether limitation is to be interpreted under 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all claim limitations together; do not dissect claims into isolated elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate claims as a whole when conducting eligibility, novelty, or obviousness analyses rather than examining isolated claim elements separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new combination of steps or elements may be patentable even if constituents were well known. In subject matter eligibility and other analyses, avoid ignoring presence of old elements within a claim when assessing the claim as a whole (citing Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure only one patent issues for the same invention to the same applicant; prevent identical subject matter from being patented more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than one patent is sought for the same invention, impose statutory double patenting rejections per MPEP § 804 and use form paragraphs 8.30–8.32 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of inventor and inventorship requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm correct identification of inventor(s) per filing date (rules differ before and after September 16, 2012) and ensure inventor(s) are properly named as applicants where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If application clearly does not name correct inventorship and applicant has not filed a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 (for AIA applications) or under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) as appropriate. See MPEP § 2109 and § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction procedures.
